name: agricultural_science_set4_p1
label: Agricultural Science: set 4 (farm animals: anatomy, nutrition, breeding, health, livestock, poultry, fish, bees and products)

papers.title: Introduction to Farm Animals: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on introduction to farm animals, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of these farm animals is a ruminant?
questions.explanation:
Ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) have one stomach with four chambers, chew the cud, and can digest the cellulose in grass with the help of microbes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Pig: The pig has a simple stomach: it is a non-ruminant (monogastric).
- Rabbit: The rabbit is a non-ruminant; it does not chew the cud.
- Chicken: The chicken is a bird with a crop and gizzard, not a ruminant.

questions.stem: Which breed of cattle is native to West Africa and tolerant of trypanosomiasis?
questions.explanation:
The N'Dama is small and hardy and survives where tsetse flies spread trypanosomiasis, which is why it is the main cattle breed in Sierra Leone.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Friesian: The Friesian is an exotic dairy breed and is very susceptible to trypanosomiasis.
- Jersey: The Jersey is an exotic dairy breed.
- Brahman: The Brahman is an exotic breed developed outside West Africa.

questions.stem: Compared with exotic breeds, local breeds of livestock are generally
questions.explanation:
Crossbreeding local and exotic animals aims to combine hardiness with productivity.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- more productive but less hardy: This describes exotic breeds: high yields of meat, milk or eggs, but less able to cope with heat, poor feed and local diseases.
- both hardier and more productive: Local breeds survive local conditions well, but grow slowly and give little milk or few eggs.
- both less hardy and less productive: Local breeds are hardier than exotic ones, which is their main advantage.

options.label: D
options.content: both less hardy and less productive

questions.stem: Goats are kept in a house at night and allowed out to graze during the day, with some extra feed given. This system of management is
questions.explanation:
For many village farmers, the semi-intensive system is the best balance: better control and growth than free range, at a cost they can afford.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- extensive: In the extensive (free-range) system, animals roam to find their own food with little housing or care.
- intensive: In the intensive system, animals are confined all the time and given all their feed.
- transhumance: Transhumance is the seasonal movement of herds in search of grazing and water.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of the extensive (free-range) system of keeping livestock?
questions.explanation:
Free-range animals also spread parasites and diseases, and can damage crops.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Housing and feed are very expensive: High housing and feed costs are a disadvantage of the intensive system.
- A lot of skilled labour is needed: The extensive system needs little labour; that is why it is cheap.
- The animals cannot be let out to find their own food: In the extensive system the animals do find their own food.

options.label: A
options.content: Animals grow slowly and are easily lost to theft, predators and disease

options.label: B
options.content: Housing and feed are very expensive

options.label: C
options.content: A lot of skilled labour is needed

options.label: D
options.content: The animals cannot be let out to find their own food

questions.stem: Which method is used to identify individual cattle in a herd?
questions.explanation:
Ear tags, ear notching, tattooing and branding identify animals, so that records of breeding, treatment and growth can be kept.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Debeaking: Debeaking is trimming the beaks of poultry to reduce pecking.
- Castration: Castration removes the testes of males not kept for breeding.
- Deworming: Deworming treats animals for internal worms.

questions.stem: Livestock in rural Sierra Leone are often called a 'bank on legs' because
questions.explanation:
Animals store wealth that grows as they grow and breed, and can be turned into cash when needed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- they earn money only from the milk they produce: Most village livestock earn money when they are sold, not from milk.
- banks lend money only to livestock farmers: This is not true and not the meaning of the saying.
- they never die or need any care: Animals can die and need feeding and health care.

options.label: A
options.content: they earn money only from the milk they produce

options.label: B
options.content: banks lend money only to livestock farmers

options.label: C
options.content: they can be sold when the family needs money, for example for school fees

options.label: D
options.content: they never die or need any care

papers.title: Animal Anatomy and Physiology: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on animal anatomy and physiology, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In a ruminant, the cellulose in grass is digested mainly in the
questions.explanation:
Bacteria and protozoa in the rumen ferment cellulose into volatile fatty acids, which the animal absorbs for energy. The microbes also make protein that the animal later digests.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- abomasum, by the animal's own enzymes: No mammal makes an enzyme that digests cellulose; the abomasum digests protein.
- omasum, by hydrochloric acid: The omasum absorbs water from the food.
- reticulum, by grinding with stones: The reticulum forms the cud; grinding with stones happens in a bird's gizzard.

options.label: A
options.content: abomasum, by the animal's own enzymes

questions.stem: Nails and other heavy objects swallowed by cattle are often trapped in the
questions.explanation:
The reticulum, with its honeycomb lining, also forms food into balls of cud that are returned to the mouth.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- rumen: The rumen is the large fermentation chamber; heavy objects pass on and lodge in the honeycomb-lined reticulum.
- omasum: The omasum absorbs water from the food.
- abomasum: The abomasum is the true stomach, which secretes acid and enzymes.

questions.stem: When a cow 'chews the cud', it is
questions.explanation:
Rumination breaks the food into small pieces with a large surface for the rumen microbes, so cellulose is digested more completely.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- chewing grass thoroughly before swallowing it for the first time: Ruminants swallow grass quickly at first; the thorough chewing comes later.
- vomiting food it cannot digest: Rumination is a normal part of digestion, not vomiting.
- grinding food with grit in its gizzard: Only birds have a gizzard.

options.label: A
options.content: chewing grass thoroughly before swallowing it for the first time

options.label: B
options.content: bringing partly digested food back to the mouth and chewing it again

options.label: D
options.content: grinding food with grit in its gizzard

questions.stem: In the digestive system of a fowl, the gizzard
questions.explanation:
Birds have no teeth, so the thick, muscular gizzard does the grinding.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- stores and softens the food: Storing and softening food is the job of the crop.
- secretes digestive enzymes and acid: Enzymes and acid are secreted by the proventriculus.
- is the common opening for droppings and eggs: The common opening is the cloaca.

options.label: C
options.content: grinds the food with grit the bird has swallowed

options.label: D
options.content: is the common opening for droppings and eggs

questions.stem: Chickens kept indoors on deep litter should be given grit because
questions.explanation:
Free-range birds pick up their own small stones; housed birds cannot, so grit must be provided.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- grit is a rich source of protein: Grit is small stones; it supplies no protein.
- grit prevents coccidiosis: Coccidiosis is prevented by dry litter and coccidiostats.
- grit keeps the litter dry: Litter is kept dry by good ventilation and fixing leaking drinkers.

options.label: A
options.content: grit is a rich source of protein

options.label: D
options.content: they have no teeth, and the gizzard needs grit to grind whole grains

questions.stem: In a bull, sperm are stored and matured in the
questions.explanation:
Testes (produce) → epididymis (store and mature) → vas deferens (carry) → urethra; the accessory glands add the fluid of the semen.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- testes: The testes produce the sperm.
- vas deferens: The vas deferens carries sperm to the urethra.
- prostate gland: The prostate is an accessory gland that adds fluid to the semen.

questions.stem: In the oviduct of a hen, the shell is added to the egg in the
questions.explanation:
Infundibulum → magnum (albumen) → isthmus (membranes) → uterus or shell gland (shell, the longest stage) → vagina → cloaca.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- infundibulum: The infundibulum catches the yolk; fertilisation takes place here.
- magnum: The magnum adds the albumen (egg white).
- isthmus: The isthmus adds the shell membranes.

papers.title: Animal Nutrition and Feeding: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on animal nutrition and feeding, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of these feedstuffs is a protein concentrate?
questions.explanation:
Protein concentrates include fish meal, groundnut cake, soya bean meal and blood meal.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Maize: Maize is an energy concentrate, rich in carbohydrate.
- Rice straw: Rice straw is a roughage: bulky, high in fibre and low in protein.
- Salt lick: A salt lick is a mineral supplement.

questions.stem: Roughages differ from concentrates in that roughages are
questions.explanation:
Roughages include fresh grass, legume forages, hay, silage, straw and crop residues.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- low in fibre and high in protein: This describes protein concentrates such as fish meal.
- fed mainly to poultry: Roughages are fed mainly to ruminants, which can digest fibre.
- always made in a feed mill: Most roughages, such as grass and straw, are not manufactured.

options.label: A
options.content: low in fibre and high in protein

options.label: C
options.content: always made in a feed mill

options.label: D
options.content: bulky, high in fibre and low in energy per kilogram

questions.stem: A farmer wants 100 kg of feed containing 16% crude protein, using maize (10% crude protein) and groundnut cake (40% crude protein). How much of each is needed?
questions.explanation:
Pearson square: maize 40 − 16 = 24 parts; groundnut cake 16 − 10 = 6 parts; total 30 parts. Maize = 24/30 × 100 = 80 kg; groundnut cake = 6/30 × 100 = 20 kg. Check: 0.8 × 10 + 0.2 × 40 = 8 + 8 = 16%.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 20 kg of maize and 80 kg of groundnut cake: The amounts are on the wrong feeds; this mix would contain 34% protein.
- 50 kg of maize and 50 kg of groundnut cake: Equal amounts give 25% protein, far more than 16%.
- 60 kg of maize and 40 kg of groundnut cake: This mix gives 22% protein, not 16%.

options.label: A
options.content: 80 kg of maize and 20 kg of groundnut cake

options.label: B
options.content: 20 kg of maize and 80 kg of groundnut cake

options.label: C
options.content: 50 kg of maize and 50 kg of groundnut cake

options.label: D
options.content: 60 kg of maize and 40 kg of groundnut cake

questions.stem: Silage is made by
questions.explanation:
The bacteria make acid that preserves the forage, so animals have feed in the dry season. Air must be kept out, or the silage rots.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- drying grass in the sun to about 15% moisture: Drying grass for storage makes hay.
- burning crop residues and storing the ash: Ash has almost no feeding value.
- mixing fresh grass with fish meal: Mixing in fish meal does not preserve grass.

options.label: A
options.content: drying grass in the sun to about 15% moisture

options.label: B
options.content: packing chopped green forage tightly in an airtight pit so that bacteria ferment it

options.label: C
options.content: burning crop residues and storing the ash

options.label: D
options.content: mixing fresh grass with fish meal

questions.stem: Dividing a pasture into paddocks that are grazed in turn, so that each can recover, is called
questions.explanation:
Rotational grazing lets the grass regrow and breaks the life cycles of some parasites.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- continuous grazing: In continuous grazing animals graze the same area all the time, which leads to overgrazing.
- zero grazing: In zero grazing (cut and carry), forage is cut and brought to housed animals.
- tethering: Tethering is tying an animal on a rope and moving it during the day.

questions.stem: If a flock of laying hens runs out of drinking water for a day, the most likely result is
questions.explanation:
Water is the cheapest and most neglected nutrient. Without it, feeding and production fall quickly, especially in hot weather.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an increase in the size of the eggs: Shortage of water reduces laying; it does not make eggs bigger.
- no effect, because hens get enough water from their feed: A laying hen drinks about twice as much water as the feed she eats.
- thicker eggshells: Shell thickness depends on calcium, not on a shortage of water.

options.label: A
options.content: an increase in the size of the eggs

options.label: B
options.content: no effect, because hens get enough water from their feed

options.label: D
options.content: a sharp fall in egg production

questions.stem: Layers' mash contains extra calcium, and oyster shell may also be given, so that the hens
questions.explanation:
An eggshell is mostly calcium carbonate. Thin-shelled eggs are a sign that the hens need more calcium.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- grow faster for meat: Fast growth for meat is the aim of broiler feeding.
- are protected against Newcastle disease: Newcastle disease is prevented by vaccination.
- lay eggs with larger yolks: Calcium is used for the shell, not the yolk.

questions.stem: Which of these is a legume grown with grasses in improved pastures?
questions.explanation:
Pasture legumes add nitrogen to the soil and raise the protein content of the forage.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Guinea grass (*Panicum maximum*): Guinea grass is a pasture grass, not a legume.
- Elephant grass (*Pennisetum purpureum*): Elephant grass is a tall pasture grass.
- *Brachiaria*: *Brachiaria* is a pasture grass.

papers.title: Animal Reproduction and Breeding: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on animal reproduction and breeding, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The gestation period of a sow is about
questions.explanation:
114 days is easy to remember as 3 months, 3 weeks and 3 days.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 31 days: About 31 days is the gestation period of a rabbit.
- 150 days: About 150 days is the gestation period of a goat.
- 283 days: About 283 days is the gestation period of a cow.

questions.stem: The surest sign that a cow is on heat is that she
questions.explanation:
Other signs are restlessness, bellowing, mounting other cows, a swollen red vulva and a clear mucus discharge.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- eats much more than usual: A cow on heat usually eats less, not more.
- lies down and refuses to move: A cow on heat is restless, not inactive.
- suddenly produces more milk: Milk yield often falls slightly during heat.

options.label: B
options.content: lies down and refuses to move

options.label: C
options.content: stands still to be mounted by other animals

questions.stem: A newborn calf, kid or piglet should receive colostrum within the first 24 hours of life because
questions.explanation:
The antibodies in colostrum give the newborn passive immunity until its own immune system develops.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- colostrum is poorer in nutrients than later milk: Colostrum is richer, not poorer, than later milk.
- the mother stops producing milk after 24 hours: The mother goes on producing milk for months.
- colostrum is the only source of iron for the young: The iron problem applies to piglets, which need an iron injection.

options.label: A
options.content: colostrum is poorer in nutrients than later milk

options.label: B
options.content: the mother stops producing milk after 24 hours

options.label: C
options.content: colostrum is the only source of iron for the young

options.label: D
options.content: colostrum contains antibodies that the young can absorb only in their first hours

questions.stem: Piglets kept on concrete floors are given an iron injection at about three days old because
questions.explanation:
Without iron, piglets become anaemic, grow slowly and may die.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- iron prevents African swine fever: Iron does not prevent this virus disease.
- iron helps their needle teeth fall out: Needle teeth are clipped; iron has nothing to do with them.
- iron replaces the colostrum they need: Piglets still need colostrum for antibodies.

options.label: A
options.content: the sow's milk contains little iron, and they cannot get iron from soil

options.label: C
options.content: iron helps their needle teeth fall out

options.label: D
options.content: iron replaces the colostrum they need

questions.stem: Mating a local N'Dama cow with a bull of a high-yielding exotic breed is an example of
questions.explanation:
Crossbred offspring often show hybrid vigour and combine the hardiness of the local breed with the productivity of the exotic one.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- inbreeding: Inbreeding is mating closely related animals.
- line breeding: Line breeding is mild inbreeding to keep the traits of one outstanding ancestor.
- selection: Selection is choosing the best animals within a breed as parents.

questions.stem: An advantage of artificial insemination (AI) over natural mating is that
questions.explanation:
AI also saves the cost of keeping a male and reduces the spread of some diseases passed on at mating.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- no trained person is needed: AI must be done by a trained technician.
- the farmer no longer needs to detect heat: Heat detection is even more important with AI, so that it is done at the right time.
- every insemination produces twins: AI does not increase the number of young per birth.

options.label: B
options.content: the farmer no longer needs to detect heat

options.label: C
options.content: semen from one outstanding male can be used to serve many females, even far away

questions.stem: How long do fertile chicken eggs take to hatch, under a broody hen or in an incubator?
questions.explanation:
An incubator must be kept at about 37.5 °C with the right humidity, and the eggs turned several times a day.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 14 days: 14 days is far too short; the chick is not fully formed.
- 28 days: 28 days is too long for chicken eggs.
- 31 days: About 31 days is the gestation period of a rabbit, not the incubation period of an egg.

papers.title: Animal Health and Disease Management: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on animal health and disease management, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Gasping, twisted necks, green diarrhoea, a fall in egg production and sudden deaths in a poultry flock are signs of
questions.explanation:
Newcastle disease is a virus disease that can kill most of a flock. It is prevented by vaccination on schedule, quarantine and hygiene.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- coccidiosis: Coccidiosis causes bloody diarrhoea and ruffled feathers.
- fowl pox: Fowl pox causes wart-like scabs on the comb and wattles.
- Gumboro disease: Gumboro causes depression and whitish diarrhoea in chicks of 3 to 6 weeks.

questions.stem: Coccidiosis in poultry is caused by
questions.explanation:
Prevention: keep litter dry, fix leaking drinkers and add coccidiostats to the feed or water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a virus spread by mosquitoes: A virus spread by mosquitoes is fowl pox.
- bacteria in clean, dry litter: Coccidiosis is not bacterial, and dry litter helps prevent it.
- a shortage of calcium in the feed: Calcium shortage causes thin eggshells and weak bones, not coccidiosis.

options.label: A
options.content: a protozoan, and outbreaks are encouraged by wet litter

options.label: D
options.content: a shortage of calcium in the feed

questions.stem: Trypanosomiasis of cattle is spread by
questions.explanation:
Trypanosomiasis causes anaemia, weakness and weight loss. Keeping trypanotolerant breeds such as the N'Dama and controlling tsetse flies are the main defences.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ticks: Ticks spread other diseases, such as babesiosis (redwater).
- mosquitoes: Mosquitoes spread fowl pox among poultry, not trypanosomiasis.
- houseflies: Houseflies carry germs onto food; they do not spread trypanosomiasis.

questions.stem: A cow dies suddenly, with dark blood oozing from its body openings, and anthrax is suspected. The farmer should
questions.explanation:
Anthrax is a bacterial disease of cattle, sheep and goats that can also kill people. It is prevented by vaccination.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- skin it quickly and sell the meat: Anthrax can infect and kill people who handle or eat the meat.
- open it to find out the cause of death: Opening the carcass lets the bacteria form spores that survive in soil for decades.
- leave it in the field for vultures: Scavengers spread the infection.

options.label: A
options.content: skin it quickly and sell the meat

options.label: B
options.content: open it to find out the cause of death

options.label: C
options.content: not open the carcass, report it, and burn or bury it deeply

options.label: D
options.content: leave it in the field for vultures

questions.stem: There is no vaccine for African swine fever. The disease is controlled mainly by
questions.explanation:
The virus can spread in uncooked pork scraps and on boots, vehicles and equipment, and kills most infected pigs. Infected herds must be slaughtered.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- treating sick pigs with antibiotics: African swine fever is caused by a virus, so antibiotics do not cure it.
- vaccinating every piglet at birth: There is no vaccine for this disease.
- deworming the pigs regularly: Deworming controls worms, not this virus.

options.label: D
options.content: strict biosecurity, and never feeding pigs uncooked kitchen swill

questions.stem: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR), a virus disease that kills many goats and sheep, is best prevented by
questions.explanation:
PPR causes fever, discharges from the eyes and nose, mouth sores, diarrhoea and pneumonia. Vaccination and isolating sick animals control it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- antibiotics: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses such as PPR.
- deworming: Deworming controls internal worms, not PPR.
- dipping: Dipping controls ticks and other external parasites, not PPR.

questions.stem: A cow has a hot, swollen, painful udder, and there are clots in her milk. She is suffering from
questions.explanation:
Mastitis is a bacterial infection of the udder. Clean milking and treatment with antibiotics control it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- milk fever: Milk fever is a shortage of calcium in the blood around calving; it causes weakness and collapse.
- foot-and-mouth disease: Foot-and-mouth disease causes blisters on the mouth and feet.
- anthrax: Anthrax usually causes sudden death.

questions.stem: New animals bought for a farm should be kept apart from the existing herd for some weeks mainly to
questions.explanation:
Quarantine gives time for any disease the new animals carry to show itself before they mix with the herd.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- let them get used to the farm's feed: They can get used to the feed while kept with the herd; isolation is for disease control.
- fatten them before they join the herd: Fattening is not the purpose of quarantine.
- allow them to breed without competition: Breeding is not the purpose of quarantine.

options.label: A
options.content: let them get used to the farm's feed

options.label: B
options.content: fatten them before they join the herd

options.label: C
options.content: make sure they do not bring a disease into the herd

options.label: D
options.content: allow them to breed without competition

papers.title: Livestock Production: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on livestock production, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Goats can cause serious damage to young trees and crops because they
questions.explanation:
Goats and sheep must be controlled, by tethering, fencing or housing, to protect crops and young trees.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- are grazers that eat only short grass: Grazing short grass close to the ground describes sheep.
- are carnivores that dig up roots for insects: Goats are herbivores.
- cannot digest grass at all: Goats can digest grass; they simply prefer to browse.

options.label: A
options.content: are grazers that eat only short grass

options.label: B
options.content: are carnivores that dig up roots for insects

options.label: D
options.content: are browsers that eat the leaves and shoots of shrubs and trees

questions.stem: Goat and sheep houses are often raised off the ground with slatted floors because
questions.explanation:
A dry, clean house reduces parasites and disease. The roof must keep out rain and the house must be well ventilated.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- goats and sheep prefer to sleep on bare earth: A dry, raised floor is healthier than damp ground.
- the slats make the house warmer: Slats are for cleanliness and dryness, not warmth.
- the animals can graze through the slats: The animals are fed inside or let out to graze; they do not graze through the floor.

options.label: A
options.content: droppings fall through, keeping the animals dry and reducing worms and foot rot

options.label: B
options.content: goats and sheep prefer to sleep on bare earth

options.label: C
options.content: the slats make the house warmer

options.label: D
options.content: the animals can graze through the slats

questions.stem: Pig pens must provide good shade because pigs
questions.explanation:
Heat-stressed pigs eat less, grow slowly and may die. Shade, ventilation and wallowing water help them keep cool.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- need sunlight to make their own iron: Pigs cannot make iron from sunlight; piglets are given iron injections.
- are browsers that feed on tree leaves: Pigs are not browsers; they eat concentrate rations.
- lose all their bristles in the sun: This is not why shade is provided.

options.label: A
options.content: need sunlight to make their own iron

options.label: B
options.content: sweat very little and suffer badly in heat

options.label: C
options.content: are browsers that feed on tree leaves

options.label: D
options.content: lose all their bristles in the sun

questions.stem: The needle teeth of piglets are clipped soon after birth in order to
questions.explanation:
Other piglet care: iron injection, castration of males not kept for breeding, and a warm, dry creep area.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- help them chew solid feed: Clipping the teeth does not help chewing.
- prevent anaemia: Anaemia is prevented by the iron injection.
- make them grow faster: Clipping the teeth does not speed growth directly; it prevents injuries.

options.label: C
options.content: stop them injuring the sow's teats and one another

questions.stem: A farmer buys 20 young goats at NLe 400 each, spends NLe 300 on each for feed and treatment, and sells each one for NLe 1000. What is the profit?
questions.explanation:
Profit per goat = 1000 − (400 + 300) = NLe 300. Total profit = 20 × 300 = NLe 6000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 12 000: This subtracts only the purchase price; the feed and treatment costs must also be taken away.
- NLe 14 000: This subtracts only the feed and treatment costs; the purchase price must also be taken away.
- NLe 20 000: This is the total sales income, before any costs are taken away.

questions.stem: Removing old, barren, sick or slow-growing animals from a herd is called
questions.explanation:
Culled animals eat feed and spread disease without producing. Culling each year and keeping the best for breeding improves the herd.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- weaning: Weaning is separating young animals from their mother's milk.
- castration: Castration is removing the testes of males.
- dehorning: Dehorning is removing horns or horn buds.

questions.stem: A goat farmer in Sierra Leone is most likely to get the best price by having well-grown animals ready to sell
questions.explanation:
Planning breeding so that animals reach a good size at the right time is part of good farm management.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- just after the festivals: Prices fall after the festivals, once the demand has passed.
- at any time, because the price of goats never changes: Goat prices rise sharply before the festivals.
- only in the middle of the rainy season: The rainy season is not when demand peaks.

options.label: A
options.content: just before Eid al-Adha and Christmas, when demand is highest

options.label: C
options.content: at any time, because the price of goats never changes

options.label: D
options.content: only in the middle of the rainy season

papers.title: Poultry Production: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on poultry production, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A poultry house is built with its long axis running east to west so that
questions.explanation:
The long sides then face north and south, with wire mesh for ventilation and a wide roof overhang against sun and rain.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the birds get direct sunlight all day: Direct sun overheats the birds; the aim is to avoid it.
- rain blows straight in to cool the birds: Rain must be kept out; wet litter causes disease.
- the house is cheaper to build: Orientation does not change the building cost.

options.label: A
options.content: the birds get direct sunlight all day

options.label: B
options.content: the sun does not shine directly in on the birds

options.label: C
options.content: rain blows straight in to cool the birds

options.label: D
options.content: the house is cheaper to build

questions.stem: Wet, caked litter around the drinkers in a poultry house is dangerous because it
questions.explanation:
Litter of wood shavings or rice husks, 5 to 10 cm deep, must be kept dry. Leaking drinkers should be fixed and wet patches removed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- makes the birds lay more eggs: Wet litter harms the birds and lowers production.
- keeps the birds cool and healthy: Wet litter breeds disease; cooling comes from ventilation.
- provides grit for the gizzard: Litter is not a source of grit.

options.label: A
options.content: makes the birds lay more eggs

options.label: B
options.content: keeps the birds cool and healthy

questions.stem: Broiler starter feed has a high protein content, about 22 to 23%, because
questions.explanation:
Broilers get starter for the first 3 to 4 weeks, then finisher until they reach market weight.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- protein gives eggs strong shells: Strong shells need calcium; and broilers are meat birds, not layers.
- protein protects chicks against Newcastle disease: Newcastle disease is prevented by vaccination.
- chicks cannot digest carbohydrate: Chicks digest carbohydrate; maize supplies most of their energy.

options.label: B
options.content: protein protects chicks against Newcastle disease

options.label: D
options.content: young broilers grow very fast and need protein to build their bodies

questions.stem: To keep laying well, layers need light for about
questions.explanation:
Day length controls the hormones that bring hens into lay. In the tropics, a few hours of artificial light are added to the natural day.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4 hours a day: 4 hours is far too little light; laying would stop.
- 8 hours a day: 8 hours is too short a day for good laying.
- 24 hours a day: Continuous light gives the birds no rest and is not needed.

questions.stem: Layers are debeaked (beak trimmed) in order to
questions.explanation:
Pecking can injure birds badly when they are crowded or stressed. Debeaking is done carefully by a trained person.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- help them pick up grit: Debeaking does not help birds pick up grit.
- stop them drinking too much water: Hens need plenty of water; debeaking is not for that.
- make them lay bigger eggs: Beak trimming does not change egg size.

options.label: C
options.content: stop them drinking too much water

questions.stem: Eggs collected for sale should be stored
questions.explanation:
Eggs should be collected at least three times a day and kept cool, so that they stay fresh until they are sold.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- in the sun with the pointed end up: Heat spoils eggs quickly, and the air cell at the blunt end should face up.
- in a warm room to keep them fresh: Warmth makes eggs go stale faster.
- with the blunt end down in a hot store: Heat spoils eggs, and the blunt end should face up.

options.label: A
options.content: in the sun with the pointed end up

options.label: B
options.content: in a cool place with the blunt end up

options.label: C
options.content: in a warm room to keep them fresh

options.label: D
options.content: with the blunt end down in a hot store

questions.stem: Brooding, in poultry management, means
questions.explanation:
Young chicks cannot keep themselves warm, so a brooder gives them heat, feed, water and protection until they are feathered.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- hatching eggs in a machine: Hatching eggs in a machine is artificial incubation.
- selling birds when they reach market weight: This is marketing, not brooding.
- removing hens that have stopped laying: Removing unproductive hens is culling.

options.label: B
options.content: selling birds when they reach market weight

options.label: C
options.content: caring for young chicks, especially keeping them warm, in their first weeks

options.label: D
options.content: removing hens that have stopped laying

questions.stem: In an 'all-in, all-out' system of poultry management,
questions.explanation:
All-in, all-out breaks the cycle of disease between batches. A footbath and limiting visitors are other parts of biosecurity.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- birds of different ages are mixed so that older birds teach the young: Mixing ages lets older birds pass diseases to younger ones.
- new birds are added whenever some die: Adding birds to an existing flock brings in disease.
- birds are let out each day and brought in at night: This describes a semi-intensive system, not all-in all-out.

options.label: A
options.content: birds of different ages are mixed so that older birds teach the young

options.label: B
options.content: new birds are added whenever some die

options.label: C
options.content: birds are let out each day and brought in at night

options.label: D
options.content: all birds of a batch arrive and leave together, and the house is cleaned and disinfected before the next batch

papers.title: Other Animal Enterprises: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on other animal enterprises, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The best soil for building a fish pond is
questions.explanation:
A good site also has a reliable supply of clean water all year and a gentle slope, so the pond can be filled and drained by gravity.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sandy soil, which drains quickly: Water would drain out of a pond built in sandy soil.
- gravelly soil: Gravel lets water seep away.
- loose topsoil full of roots: Loose, root-filled soil cannot be compacted to make watertight banks.

options.label: A
options.content: clay or clay loam, which holds water

questions.stem: A new fish pond is fertilised with manure before stocking in order to
questions.explanation:
Acidic ponds are limed first. Then manure feeds the plankton, which feed the fish.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- kill any wild fish in the pond: Wild fish are kept out by screens on the inlet, not by manure.
- make the water clearer: Fertilising makes the water greener with plankton, not clearer.
- raise the water temperature: Manure is added to feed the plankton, not to warm the water.

options.label: A
options.content: kill any wild fish in the pond

options.label: B
options.content: grow plankton, the natural food of young fish

questions.stem: Fish in an overstocked pond that is also overfed often die suddenly around dawn. The main reason is that
questions.explanation:
At night, plants and plankton use oxygen instead of producing it, so oxygen is lowest at dawn. Stock and feed at the recommended rates.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the water becomes too cold at night: Pond water does not cool enough at night to kill tropical fish.
- plankton poisons them at dawn: Plankton is their food; the problem is the lack of oxygen.
- birds eat them at dawn: Predators take some fish, but they do not cause sudden mass deaths.

options.label: A
options.content: the water becomes too cold at night

options.label: C
options.content: decaying feed and many fish use up the oxygen in the water

questions.stem: In a honeybee colony, the sterile females that collect nectar and pollen and make honey and wax are the
questions.explanation:
Workers also build comb, feed the young, and guard and clean the hive.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- queen: The queen is the only fertile female; she lays all the eggs.
- drones: Drones are males whose role is to mate with a new queen.
- brood: The brood are the eggs, larvae and pupae developing in the comb.

questions.stem: A beekeeper uses a smoker when opening a hive to harvest honey in order to
questions.explanation:
Harvest in the early morning or evening, wear protective clothing, take only ripe, capped comb and leave enough honey for the bees.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- kill the bees: Smoke calms bees; killing them would destroy the colony.
- dry the honey: Honey is not dried with smoke.
- flavour the honey: Smoke is not used to flavour honey.

questions.stem: In rabbit keeping, 'kindling' means
questions.explanation:
A nest box with dry grass is put in the hutch a few days before kindling. Litters are usually 6 to 8.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- mating: Mating is called serving; kindling comes about 31 days later.
- weaning the young: Weaning is taking the young off their mother's milk, at about 6 weeks.
- building the hutch: Building the hutch is not called kindling.

questions.stem: Snails reared in a snailery are given crushed shells or limestone in order to
questions.explanation:
Snails also need shade, moist but not waterlogged soil, leaves and fruit, and protection from ants, rats and other predators.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- keep the soil in the pen dry: Snails need moist soil; limestone is fed for calcium, not used to dry the soil.
- help them digest cellulose: Calcium does not help digestion of cellulose.
- make them lay eggs in water: Snails lay their eggs in the soil, not in water.

options.label: A
options.content: keep the soil in the pen dry

options.label: C
options.content: supply the calcium they need for strong shells

options.label: D
options.content: make them lay eggs in water

papers.title: Animal Products and Processing: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on animal products and processing, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Pasteurisation of milk
questions.explanation:
Milk is heated to about 63 °C for 30 minutes, or about 72 °C for 15 seconds, then cooled quickly.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- removes all the fat from the milk: Fat is separated by skimming or a separator, not by pasteurisation.
- adds bacteria that turn the milk into yoghurt: Adding lactic acid bacteria makes yoghurt; pasteurisation kills bacteria.
- freezes the milk solid: Pasteurisation heats milk; it does not freeze it.

options.label: A
options.content: removes all the fat from the milk

options.label: B
options.content: adds bacteria that turn the milk into yoghurt

options.label: D
options.content: heats the milk enough to kill harmful bacteria without boiling it

questions.stem: When an egg is placed in a bowl of water, it stands on end or floats. This shows that the egg is
questions.explanation:
As an egg ages, water is lost through the shell and the air cell at the blunt end grows, so the egg becomes lighter for its size.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- fresh, because fresh eggs float: A fresh egg sinks and lies flat.
- fertile, because fertile eggs float: Floating is a sign of age, not fertility.
- hard-boiled: Boiling does not make an egg float.

options.label: A
options.content: stale, because its air cell has grown larger

questions.stem: Shining a bright light through an egg in a dark room, to check for cracks, blood spots and the size of the air cell, is called
questions.explanation:
Candling also shows whether an egg is fertile, which is used to remove infertile eggs from an incubator.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- grading: Grading sorts eggs by size, cleanliness and shell quality.
- incubation: Incubation keeps fertile eggs warm until they hatch.
- pasteurisation: Pasteurisation is heat treatment of milk.

questions.stem: In the leather trade, the word 'skins' is used for the coverings of
questions.explanation:
Hides and skins must be removed carefully, without cuts, and cured promptly by salting or drying to keep their value.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- large animals such as cattle: The coverings of large animals are called hides.
- fish: Fish skins are not what the leather trade means by skins.
- poultry: Poultry are plucked; their skins are not used for leather.

options.label: C
options.content: small animals such as goats and sheep

questions.stem: Bone meal is added to animal feed mainly as a source of
questions.explanation:
Calcium and phosphorus build bones and, in layers, eggshells. Bone meal is also used as a fertiliser.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- protein: Protein by-products include blood meal, fish meal and feather meal.
- energy: Energy comes mainly from grains such as maize.
- vitamin A: Vitamin A comes from green forage, fish oil and premixes.

questions.stem: Improved fish-smoking ovens are encouraged in coastal towns such as Tombo because they
questions.explanation:
Most fish processors are women who spend long hours by the ovens, so less smoke protects their health, and less wood saves forests.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- smoke the fish without any heat: Smoking always uses heat from a fire.
- add salt to the fish as it smokes: Salting is a separate method of preservation.
- turn the fish into fish meal: Fish meal is made by drying and grinding low-grade fish and waste.

options.label: A
options.content: use less firewood and produce less smoke for the processors

options.label: B
options.content: smoke the fish without any heat

options.label: C
options.content: add salt to the fish as it smokes

options.label: D
options.content: turn the fish into fish meal

questions.stem: Meat should be inspected before it is sold mainly to
questions.explanation:
Meat should come from an inspected slaughter place, and be kept cold or preserved by smoking, drying, salting or canning.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- fix the price of the meat: Prices are set by the market, not by inspection.
- make the meat more tender: Inspection checks safety; it does not change tenderness.
- add preservatives to the meat: Inspectors check meat; they do not add preservatives.

options.label: A
options.content: fix the price of the meat

options.label: B
options.content: stop diseases such as anthrax, tuberculosis and tapeworms reaching consumers
